source_text: Ideo autem dixi eloquiis te usum omnino Manichaei, quia etsi in apostoli Ioannis Epistola nonnulla ex his verba teneantur; tamen quia certum est, non ibi illum Ecclesiae magistrum aut de carne, aut de sensu carnis, aut de concupiscentia nuptiali, quidquam tale sensisse, quale Manichaeus verborum eius usurpatione componit; non iniuria eius verba esse dixi, cuius sensui serviebant, ut eloquia intentionis suae merito censeantur; et sicut apud sanctum Ioannem apostolica sunt dignitate reverenda, quia insinuant veritatem, ita apud Manichaeum obumbrata illorum signa non expressa videantur.
pass_a_gloss: But I have said that you have used the utterances of Manichaeus altogether, because even if some of these words are held in the Apostle John's Letter, nevertheless, because it is certain that that teacher of the Church sensed nothing there either about flesh, or about the sensation of the flesh, or about nuptial desire of such a kind as Manichaeus composes by usurping his words, I said not unjustly that they are the words of him whose sense they were serving, so that the utterances may deservedly be judged of his intention; and just as with the holy John they are to be revered with apostolic dignity, because they insinuate the truth, so with Manichaeus the overshadowed signs of those words may seem not expressed.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS nuptiae; Blaise Christian marriage as God's work
LS meritum; Blaise; glossary: desert not treasury-of-merit

pass_b_english: I said that you used language entirely belonging to Manichaeus because, although some of these words occur in the apostle John’s letter, it is certain that this teacher of the Church meant nothing there about the flesh, its sensation, or marital desire like what Manichaeus constructs by appropriating his words. I therefore rightly called them the words of the man whose meaning they served: language should be judged according to the intention behind it. In Saint John these words deserve reverence for their apostolic dignity, because they convey truth; in Manichaeus they appear as obscured traces of those words, not their faithful expression.

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
